blindSummary:
Gender transition is not explicitly criminalised in this country, but a rights-group review documents that it is effectively criminalised through three indecency provisions of the penal code, and NGOs have documented arrests of LGBT+ people under these provisions. Same-sex activity itself carries up to 2 years. There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, and no visible community infrastructure — activism operates almost entirely underground.

Unlike neighbouring states, this country lacks even a documented trans-visitor incident — partly because very few tourists visit and researchers have limited access. The legal exposure for a visibly trans visitor (indecency arrest) is real but the enforcement pattern is thinner than the entrapment machinery documented in one neighbouring state or the 2024-25 arrest wave in another.
blindOutOfScope: Indecency-law application to trans people is documented in aggregate, not per-case; tourism volume is very low.
blindSourceSummaries: Regional rights-group country review: gender transition is not explicitly criminalised but is effectively criminalised under three penal-code indecency provisions; no legal framework for gender-affirming healthcare means doctors could be prosecuted under other penal-code provisions; no legal gender recognition - a court denied a plaintiff's gender-marker correction citing religious law and prevailing social norms.

A foreign home ministry's country-of-origin bulletin on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (July 2026): same-sex activity penalised under one penal-code provision (up to 2 years) and 'public indecency' under another (up to 3 years), applying to men and women; LGBT+ people are a particular social group; those fearing the state are unlikely to obtain protection or relocate internally.

Fact-checking outlet (Aug 2024): confirms the claim that this country prohibits gender transitions and trans identity - homosexuality is criminalised and gender-affirming medical/surgical care is not available; published during a 2024 international controversy over the eligibility of one of the country's female athletes to compete in a major sporting event.

A foreign government's 2023 human-rights report on this country: official assessment including the SOGI section - one penal-code provision criminalises same-sex activity (up to 2 years) and another 'public indecency' provision carries up to 3 years; documents arrests and prosecutions of LGBT people.

International LGBTI organisation's world survey of laws criminalising same-sex activity (May 2008): global survey of criminalisation laws, with this country's entry covering its two penal-code indecency provisions.
An international rights group (Oct 2020): reports mass convictions for homosexuality in this country — 44 people convicted in a provincial-city case.

Public broadcaster survey-data feature on the region (June 2019), drawing on a regional social-attitudes poll of 25,000+ people: acceptance of homosexuality is low or extremely low across the region (as low as 6% in one surveyed country); rising irreligiosity among youth; this country was the exception on acceptance of women in leadership - regional social-attitudes context.
blindTangential: Same-sex activity carries up to 2 years under an indecency provision of the penal code — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
